What I'm seeing across the industry right now is that the biggest bottleneck to AI adoption isn't model capabilities. It's data infrastructure.

Today, we're expanding the Eon Data Foundation with the launch of Eon Yukon, a new serverless data engine purposely built to change that.

AI agents need fresh, contextualized data to act.
Specialized models need a continuous feed of data and feedback to improve. Both are still served by a stack, an architecture, and methods built for dashboards:

-Spark and Flink clusters sized for peak, plus compaction jobs to keep tables usable.

-A pipeline and a copy for every consumer, staged bronze to silver to gold.

-Hand-written jobs, wired together by an orchestrator and kept alive by specialists.

The result: shipping data is complicated, risky, and expensive. While coding agents ship apps in hours, they rarely build or run data pipelines. The data is too volatile, and a mistake costs too much.

With Yukon, data moves from ingestion to processing to serving in one continuous flow, without the infrastructure and pipelines traditionally required to connect them.

Events become compacted, sorted, deduplicated Iceberg tables within seconds.

Real-time aggregations run inline, with fully managed state. Agents and applications can access fresh data with sub-millisecond latency through a Redis-compatible API or through our SQL and spark compatible query engine.

Beyond moving and serving data, Yukon makes it continuously understandable - Live column-level statistics, accessible through MCP, give agents visibility into the data. Built-in monitoring, sampling, and data minimization help teams maintain control.

At 1M events/sec and equal freshness, Yukon used 4x less compute than Spark and 7x less than Flink. The benchmark is public: run it yourself with Eon’s ingest-bench.

This is another major step toward our vision of an Autonomous Data Foundation for the AI era, built to both protect enterprise data and unlock its full potential.

INFLEQTION SAYS IT WILL HAVE A TRULY USEFUL QUANTUM COMPUTER BY 2028

Quantum computers are built from qubits. Most qubits make a lot of mistakes. To fix that, companies group several of them together into one reliable "logical qubit." Logical qubits are the ones that actually matter.

Infleqtion just built 30 logical qubits using only 80 regular ones, per Forbes. Most approaches need far more raw qubits to get there.

Its goal is 100 logical qubits by 2028. That's around the point where quantum computers could start solving problems no regular computer can.

The trick is how it builds them. Infleqtion uses individual atoms held in place by lasers, and every atom can talk to every other atom. Most big players use superconducting chips that need giant freezers and can only connect neighbors.

Those chips are faster, but they need way more steps to do the same work. CTO Pranav Gokhale says that shrinks their speed edge from about 1,000x to about 10x.

"What really matters is if we get to 100 logical qubits near-term as planned. I think that will be a challenge for superconducting systems."

It's already making money too, selling ultra-precise atomic clocks and sensors. It raised more than $500M in its IPO this year and expects about $45M in revenue in 2026.

SOME PERSONAL THOUGHTS AHEAD OF WEEKEND

I wanted to share a few thoughts heading into the weekend because at least for me this has been one of most mentally exhausting stretches I've experienced investing in growth stocks.

And honestly one of the things I've found most difficult has very little to do with market itself since it's how much mental real estate I apparently occupy in the minds of certain "gurus" on this platform whom I've never met, followed or even spoken to.

I started sharing my thoughts on X back in 2023 simply because I genuinely love investing and wanted somewhere to talk about market, share my research and connect with people who enjoyed it as much as I did and I never imagined that would turn into an account reaching 100 million impressions every month or that I'd eventually find myself appearing on national television every week.

I'm incredibly grateful because this platform accelerated my career at a relatively young age and opened doors that otherwise might have taken me many more years to reach but I'd be lying if I said spotlight wasn't intense since the larger my audience becomes and more visible I am the more I've realized that success also seems to attract resentment from people I've never interacted with or affected in any way possible.

Daniel has a phrase for this that I think captures it perfectly because "hating up" is absolutely real especially online where people seem more comfortable attacking someone who has become visible than examining why that person's success bothers them in the first place.

Like I've had people accuse me of taking an investment idea from them despite fact that I don't follow them and have never even seen their work while others take a disagreement over a particular thesis and turn it into a personal judgment about whether I know anything about investing.

What I find especially strange is that some of these individuals are in their 40s and 50s have been doing this for decades and still seem determined to tear down a 33 year old who is simply willing to publish his research, explain what he believes and put his own money behind those convictions (I've never asked anyone to agree with me or suggested that my way of investing is the only way to succeed).

And I think that last part is important because I do all of this under my real name and face, publicly disclose what I own through my subs service, share my position sizes and actual dollars I've invested and expose myself to scrutiny over every good decision and every mistake along the way.

There's absolutely nothing wrong with choosing to remain anonymous and I respect anyone who prefers to operate that way but theres just a different level of personal accountability when people know exactly who you are and watch you explain your thesis on camera and follow your positions in real time and wait for first opportunity to use a bad outcome against you... just remember being wrong privately costs you money but being wrong publicly can also cost you reputation, confidence and peace of mind which is something I don't think people fully appreciate until they've experienced it themselves.

None of this is to suggest that criticism should be off limits because disagreement is a huge part of investing but what I truly struggle to understand is why disagreement so often has to become personal... especially during periods like this when so many people are already dealing with painful drawdowns and questioning decisions they made with the best information available to them.

Markets eventually humble every single one of us regardless of how experienced we are or how much success we've had and anyone who stays in this long enough will eventually experience a thesis that breaks or a position they sized too aggressively or a drawdown that exposes a weakness in their process or a decision they wish they could take back so that's why I think showing people grace matters so much because you never know when you'll find yourself on the other side of that experience hoping others will extend you the same understanding.

And also just remember it cost absolutely nothing to root for people, respect the work they're putting in and recognize that someone can be wrong about an investment without deserving to be ridiculed for it and I genuinely wish more people on this platform understood that being publicly wrong doesn't erase courage it takes to stand behind your own convictions in the first place.

And to the people who've made rooting against me a hobby I genuinely hope you find the same energy for your own work that you've found for mine because if you're spending more time waiting for someone else to fail than building something of your own then maybe my portfolio isn't what needs your attention.

I'll be here next week, same name, same face, same conviction.

Key takeaways from my latest industry survey and research conclusions:

1. Order visibility and shipment plans:
Strong new orders from OpenAI and Anthropic have extended Google TPU shipment visibility to 2029, ahead of Nvidia GPUs and other AI ASICs (mostly 4Q27–2Q28).

(1) From 2028, v9 will become the mainstay of Google’s own compute buildout, so v8-series orders (8t / 8i or their design variants) can be viewed as coming from OpenAI and Anthropic.

(2) Combined 2028–2029 demand: about 12M units for OpenAI (8t, designed by MediaTek) and about 14M for Anthropic (8i, designed by Broadcom), with both growing year over year. OpenAI buys outright, while Anthropic uses a mix of leasing and outright purchases.

(3) Given supply chain constraints, more reasonable TPU shipment estimates for 2027–2029 are 8–9M, 14–15M, and 16–18M units, respectively. The market broadly expects AI capex to peak in 2028, yet this plan shows TPU shipments still growing in 2029, driven by direct orders from AI service leaders OpenAI and Anthropic.

2. v10 lineup and supply chain changes:
v10 has changed from Icefish and Merope / Bladerunner to Quillfish, with mass production expected in 2029. MediaTek has won the design service order.

(1) Icefish is now v11, with mass production expected in 2030 and the design service order also going to MediaTek. Merope has lower visibility: no supplier has been chosen, and it may be canceled.

(2) MediaTek will be the sole supplier for v9 (Humufish & Triggerfish) and v10 (Quillfish), accounting for about 45–50%, 50–55%, and 55–60% of total TPU supply in 2027–2029, respectively. TPU’s contribution to its revenue and profit should rise each year.

(3) From v9 onward, all new TPUs use Intel’s EMIB-T advanced packaging. Given limited initial production capacity, the v8 series should remain the bulk of TPU shipments through 2029. v8 is expected to be the main source of TPU profit growth for MediaTek and Broadcom over the next few years, thanks to significant accumulated learning-curve benefits and the fact that both handle procurement of key components and materials.

3. Market attention and supplier outlook:
Recent events should raise and sustain market attention on Google TPU, with key design service providers MediaTek and Broadcom likely to be the supply chain’s top focus.

(1) Uncertainty over Nvidia’s CEO succession helps Google in discussing post-2028 long-term plans with customers. OpenAI and Anthropic are both key TPU customers, so their IPOs should also raise and sustain attention on TPU, and MediaTek and Broadcom are the suppliers the market most readily associates with it.

(2) MediaTek is clearly the biggest TPU winner of the next few years. Its position as sole design supplier from v9 onward, together with a supply share that rises each year alongside TPU shipments, will expand its TPU revenue. The high-margin 8t series, with shipment visibility through 2029, is a key profit source.

(3) Because Broadcom leads the 8i design, its gross margin is even higher than the 8t’s, supporting Broadcom’s profit growth. Note, however, that Broadcom’s focus over the next few years will be non-TPU XPU and AI networking chip orders, with non-TPU revenue expected to surpass TPU revenue as early as 2027.
